title: A droop at breakfast
objective: Recognize stroke as an emergency: find out when the client was last known well, because treatment is time-sensitive
secondaryObjectives: Know that hemorrhagic stroke is most often caused by hypertension and that anticoagulants raise the risk

brief.situation: 08:15 in a long-term care home. You are the LPN on the west hall. The aide calls you to Mr. Haddad, 74, who 'can't hold his spoon and is talking funny' at breakfast. He has hypertension and atrial fibrillation and takes an anticoagulant.
handover: The night aide checked him at 06:00 and says he 'said good morning like always' when she helped him to the bathroom.
He is sitting up in his chair with his breakfast tray and his morning pills in a cup in front of him.
Facility policy: for suspected stroke the nurse calls 911 at once, notifies the RN supervisor and the provider, keeps the resident NPO, notes the last-known-well time, and sends the medication list.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What is happening to Mr. Haddad, and what do you do within your role?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Facial droop, arm drift and slurred speech are stroke signs; treatment is time-sensitive and depends on when he was last known well (06:00), not when he was found; his anticoagulant and high blood pressure raise the risk of a bleed.
parts.modelAnswer: That's a stroke until proven otherwise: the droop, the arm drift and the slurred speech. What matters is when he was last normal, 06:00, not when we found him. On a blood thinner with that pressure, it could be a bleed.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Keeps him NPO, finds the last-known-well time, calls 911 and the RN supervisor at once, takes vital signs and glucose, and sends the medication list with the anticoagulant time.
parts.modelAnswer: Nothing by mouth, get the last-known-well time, call 911 and the RN now, check his vitals and sugar, and send his med list with the time of his last blood thinner.

scoring.modelReasoning: Sudden face drooping, arm weakness and slurred speech are stroke warning signs; call 911 right away. The time symptoms first appeared, or when the person was last known well, decides treatment, and the treatments that work best are available only if stroke is recognized and diagnosed within hours. Within the LPN role: keep him NPO (his swallow may be impaired), establish last known well (06:00), call 911 and the RN supervisor under facility policy, check vital signs and glucose, and send the medication list with the last anticoagulant dose; hypertension and anticoagulants raise the risk of a hemorrhagic stroke.
